Clinical Reference · Pulmonology / ID

Hospital-Acquired & Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia

On this page
Pneumonia that develops ≥48 h after hospital admission (HAP) or >48 h after endotracheal intubation (VAP) — driven by microaspiration of colonizing hospital flora past compromised airway defenses. Every empiric regimen must cover S. aureus and Pseudomonas; treat for 7 days and de-escalate to cultures.
HAP ≥48 h · VAP >48 h post-intubation Prior IV antibiotics <90 d = key MDR risk 7-day therapy (IDSA/ATS 2016) VAP attributable mortality ≈13% HCAP category retired
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story

In a healthy person the lower airway is nearly sterile because three defenses guard it: the glottis/cough reflex, the mucociliary escalator, and alveolar macrophages/neutrophils. Hospitalization and critical illness dismantle all three, and the final common event is microaspiration of colonized secretions into the distal airway.

  1. The endotracheal tube stents the glottis open. The one-way valve that protects the lungs is gone. Colonized oropharyngeal and gastric secretions pool above the cuff and leak down microchannels along the cuff folds — “microaspiration past the cuff.”
  2. Biofilm on the tube. Bacteria coat the tube lumen in a polysaccharide biofilm — a fortress shielding them from antibiotics and immunity — which embolizes distally with suctioning and airflow.
  3. Impaired mucociliary clearance. Sedation, high FiO₂, positive pressure and the tube itself paralyze the escalator, so any inoculum that arrives is not swept out.
  4. Gastric & oropharyngeal colonization. Acid suppression, supine positioning and enteral feeds convert the low-biomass stomach into a reservoir of gram-negative bacilli that colonize the mouth and get aspirated.
  5. Immunoparalysis of critical illness. The alveolar macrophage/neutrophil response is blunted, so a small inoculum establishes invasive infection → neutrophilic exudate fills alveoli → consolidation → V/Q mismatch, hypoxemia, and cytokine-driven fever, leukocytosis and sepsis.
the healthy airway is a castle: the glottis is the drawbridge, cough is the boiling oil, and cilia are servants sweeping the floors. Intubation jams the drawbridge permanently open, dumps the oil, and drugs the servants asleep, while biofilm on the tube is an enemy camp already inside the outer wall. Antibiotics are reinforcements sent after the invaders breach — which is why prevention (keeping the drawbridge working) beats treatment.
Microaspiration cascade: how hospitalization/intubation converts colonization into invasive pneumonia. Source: IDSA/ATS 2016 (Kalil).
Bronchopneumonia histology: alveoli and bronchioles packed with neutrophil-rich purulent exudate — the airway-centered acute inflammation of bacterial nosocomial pneumonia.
Mikael Häggström, M.D. · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons
every antibiotic used in HAP/VAP interrupts one specific step of bacterial survival. β-lactams (pip-tazo, cefepime, ceftazidime, meropenem, imipenem, aztreonam) block cell-wall cross-linking at penicillin-binding proteins → osmotic lysis. Vancomycin binds the D-Ala-D-Ala peptidoglycan terminus (same wall, different rung). Linezolid jams the 50S ribosome to stop protein synthesis. Aminoglycosides corrupt the 30S ribosome (misreading). Fluoroquinolones poison DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV. Polymyxins shred the gram-negative outer membrane. Keep this map in mind — it explains every drug choice downstream.
Drug classMolecular target / mechanismAgents in HAP/VAP
β-lactamsInhibit cell-wall synthesis via penicillin-binding proteins (transpeptidases) → defective peptidoglycan → lysisPip-tazo, cefepime, ceftazidime, meropenem, imipenem, aztreonam
GlycopeptidesBind D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of peptidoglycan precursors → block cross-linking (gram-positive)Vancomycin
OxazolidinonesBind 50S ribosome (23S rRNA) → block 70S initiation complex → stop protein synthesisLinezolid
AminoglycosidesBind 30S ribosome → misreading → inhibit protein synthesis (concentration-dependent)Amikacin, gentamicin, tobramycin
FluoroquinolonesInhibit DNA gyrase (topo II) & topo IV → block DNA replicationCiprofloxacin, levofloxacin
PolymyxinsBind lipid A of LPS → disrupt gram-negative outer membrane → leakage/death (salvage)Colistin, polymyxin B

Mechanism map: Kalil AC et al., Clin Infect Dis 2016;63:e61 — IDSA/ATS 2016 HAP/VAP guideline.

Definitions & classification

TermDefinitionKey point
HAPPneumonia not incubating at admission, occurring ≥48 h after admission, in a patient not mechanically ventilated at diagnosis.Non-ventilated by definition.
VAPPneumonia occurring >48 h after endotracheal intubation.Ventilated patient with new pneumonia.
HCAPRetired in 2016. “Healthcare-associated pneumonia” poorly predicted MDR organisms and drove over-broad antibiotics.Nursing-home/dialysis patients now handled under CAP + individual MDR risk.
Early- vs late-onset<5 d: more community-type, susceptible organisms. ≥5 d: more MDR gram-negatives & MRSA.2016 guideline de-emphasizes timing in favor of individual MDR risk factors.
VAE surveillance ≠ clinical VAPThe CDC/NHSN Ventilator-Associated Event ladder is an objective surveillance tool, not a bedside diagnosis: VAC = after ≥2 stable days, a sustained rise in FiO₂ ≥0.20 or PEEP ≥3 cm H₂O for ≥2 days → IVAC adds temp <36/>38 °C or WBC ≤4/≥12 plus a new antimicrobial ≥4 days → PVAP adds microbiologic evidence. Source: CDC/NHSN VAE protocol.
🦠

Microbiology — who causes it

The organisms that matter are the two mandatory empiric targets plus the MDR gram-negatives that emerge with time and antibiotic pressure:

  • Staphylococcus aureus — MSSA and MRSA (leading gram-positive).
  • Pseudomonas aeruginosa — leading gram-negative in VAP; predilection for structural lung disease.
  • Enterobacterales — Klebsiella (incl. ESBL/carbapenemase), E. coli, Enterobacter (AmpC), Serratia.
  • Non-fermenters — Acinetobacter baumannii, Stenotrophomonas maltophilia (intrinsically MDR).
  • Streptococcus spp. and H. influenzae — more in early-onset disease.
Gram-negative rods of Pseudomonas aeruginosa on Gram stain of BAL fluid — a leading MDR cause of VAP; the Gram stain guides early empiric choice.
Ajay Kumar Chaurasiya · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Gram-positive cocci of Staphylococcus aureus in grape-like clusters — MSSA/MRSA is a common cause of HAP/VAP and the reason MRSA cover is added when risk factors are present.

📊

Presentation — signs, frequency & why they happen

Diagnosis requires a new/progressive radiographic infiltrate PLUS ≥2 clinical features (fever, leukocytosis/leukopenia, purulent secretions, worsening oxygenation). Frequencies below are approximate teaching estimates in suspected HAP/VAP (color: red >70%, amber 40–70%, blue 15–40%, purple <15%).

Feature~FrequencyWhy it happens (pathophysiology)
New/progressive infiltrate on imaging100%*Alveolar filling by neutrophilic exudate — required diagnostic criterion (*by definition).
Purulent tracheobronchial secretions~75%Neutrophil-rich exudate expelled from infected airways; abundant, discolored on suctioning.
Worsening oxygenation (↑FiO₂/PEEP need, ↓P:F)~75%Consolidated alveoli create intrapulmonary shunt → V/Q mismatch → hypoxemia.
Fever >38 °C~65%Pyrogenic cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF) reset the hypothalamic set-point; may be blunted by sedation/antipyretics.
Leukocytosis (>12) or leukopenia (<4)~60%Marrow neutrophil release; leukopenia signals overwhelming sepsis and marrow exhaustion (worse prognosis).
Tachypnea / increased work of breathing~60%Hypoxemia + acidosis drive respiratory rate; stiff consolidated lung raises the work of breathing.
New crackles / bronchial breath sounds~55%Airflow through fluid-filled, consolidated alveoli; hard to appreciate on a ventilated patient.
Hemodynamic instability / septic shock~20–30%Cytokine-driven vasodilation + capillary leak → distributive shock; marks “high mortality risk.”
Hemoptysis / cavitation<10%Tissue necrosis from virulent organisms (MRSA, Pseudomonas, Klebsiella) → necrotizing pneumonia/abscess.
None of these is specific in a ventilated patient — ARDS, atelectasis, aspiration pneumonitis, PE and pulmonary edema all mimic VAP. That non-specificity is exactly why the guideline says don’t use CPIS or procalcitonin to start antibiotics; treat on the composite clinical picture and cultures.
🩺 Clinic — post-acute care, prevention & recognition
Assess

Who is at risk & when to suspect

🔍

The outpatient / post-acute lens

True HAP/VAP is inpatient by definition, but the clinic and post-acute settings own three jobs: preventing nosocomial and aspiration pneumonia, recognizing it early in patients in SNF/LTAC or recently discharged, and knowing that a hospitalization or IV antibiotics within 90 days is the single strongest MDR risk factor when these patients bounce back.

  • Highest-risk outpatients: residents of SNF/LTAC, patients on home mechanical ventilation or tracheostomy, recent hospitalization/IV antibiotics within 90 days, dysphagia/stroke/dementia (aspiration), immunosuppression, structural lung disease (bronchiectasis, COPD).
  • HCAP is dead: do not reflexively give broad MDR coverage to every nursing-home patient. Work them up as CAP and layer MDR coverage only if they have real risk factors (prior IV abx 90 d, prior MDR isolate, poor functional status with prior colonization).
  • Suspect it when: a post-acute or recently-discharged patient has new cough/dyspnea/purulent sputum + fever or hypoxia, especially with a witnessed aspiration event or feeding-tube use.

a genuine new infiltrate + hypoxia + systemic illness in a post-acute patient is not an outpatient disease. Confirm oxygenation and imaging, then admit — the clinic’s value here is fast recognition and disposition, not outpatient antibiotics.
Prevent

Prevention ladder

🛡️

First-line habits → targeted interventions

prevention works upstream of every antibiotic in this guide — it keeps colonized secretions out of the lower airway (aspiration precautions, oral care, HOB elevation) and shrinks the reservoir (deprescribing unnecessary acid suppression, treating dysphagia).
1
Universal, low-cost measures
Every at-risk post-acute patient.
▾
  • Aspiration precautions: keep head of bed elevated, upright for meals/tube feeds, dysphagia-appropriate diet textures.
  • Oral care & dental hygiene: reduces the oropharyngeal bacterial reservoir.
  • Early mobility & incentive spirometry: preserve the mucociliary escalator and lung recruitment.
  • Deprescribe unnecessary PPIs/H2 blockers: gastric acid suppression enlarges the gram-negative reservoir — stop when there is no ongoing indication.
  • Smoking cessation: restores ciliary function and mucosal defense.
2
Vaccination
Reduce the pneumonias you can prevent.
▾
  • Pneumococcal: PCV20 alone, or PCV15 followed by PPSV23, for all adults ≥65 and younger adults with chronic lung/heart/liver disease, diabetes, or immunocompromise (ACIP).
  • Influenza: annually — influenza is a major precursor to bacterial (esp. S. aureus) pneumonia.
  • COVID-19 and, where indicated, RSV vaccination in older/comorbid adults.
3
Targeted / specialist
Recurrent or high-risk patients.
▾
  • Formal swallow evaluation (SLP) and modified-diet/feeding strategy for recurrent aspiration.
  • Tracheostomy/home-vent care protocols: inline suctioning, cuff-pressure management, caregiver training.
  • Pulmonary referral for bronchiectasis/structural lung disease with recurrent gram-negative infection.

Escalate

When to send to the ED / admit

🚑

Red flags → do not manage as outpatient

SpO₂ <92% or new oxygen requirement · respiratory rate ≥30 · SBP <90 or signs of shock · altered mental status / new confusion · inability to maintain oral intake or secretions · prior IV antibiotics within 90 days with a new infiltrate (MDR-risk pneumonia that needs inpatient broad-spectrum therapy) · rapidly progressive or multilobar infiltrate.

Any of these means the patient needs the Wards pathway (or ICU if unstable) — proceed to the inpatient panels.

🛏️ Wards — hospital-acquired pneumonia (non-ventilated)
Admit

Recognizing HAP on the floor

📋

Diagnosis & the two decisions that set therapy

Diagnose HAP when an inpatient ≥48 h into admission develops a new/progressive infiltrate + ≥2 of fever, leukocytosis/leukopenia, purulent secretions, or worsening oxygenation. Two questions then determine the empiric regimen:

  1. Is there MRSA risk? — prior IV antibiotics within 90 days, or a unit where >10–20% of S. aureus is MRSA (or unknown).
  2. Is there high mortality risk or MDR-Pseudomonas risk? — need for ventilatory support due to the pneumonia, septic shock, structural lung disease, or prior IV antibiotics. This drives whether you use double antipseudomonal coverage.
Mandatory targetsEvery empiric HAP regimen must cover S. aureus, P. aeruginosa, and other gram-negative bacilli — the floor patient still gets an antipseudomonal backbone. Source: Kalil 2016.

Treat

Empiric antibiotic therapy

💊

Escalation ladder — single agent → add MRSA → dual coverage

the ladder mirrors risk. Everyone gets an antipseudomonal β-lactam (cell-wall attack on the dominant gram-negatives). Add a ribosome/cell-wall anti-MRSA agent when S. aureus resistance is likely, and add a second, different-class gram-negative agent when MDR Pseudomonas is likely so that at least one drug is active while cultures are pending.

1
Baseline: one antipseudomonal β-lactam
Low MRSA risk, low MDR risk, unit resistance <10%.
▾

Pick ONE antipseudomonal agent — it also covers MSSA and the common Enterobacterales.

DrugStart (normal renal fxn)Adjust / maxWhy it worksIf allergic / alt
Piperacillin-tazobactam4.5 g IV q6hExtended infusion over 4 h; renal-doseβ-lactam + BLI; antipseudomonal + anaerobe coverCefepime or (severe allergy) aztreonam + vanc
Cefepime2 g IV q8hRenal-dose; watch neurotoxicity in renal failureAntipseudomonal cephalosporin; PBP inhibitorAztreonam (shares side chain w/ ceftazidime — avoid if that's the allergen)
Meropenem1 g IV q8hRenal-dose; lower seizure risk than imipenemCarbapenem — broadest β-lactam, ESBL coverReserve for ESBL/high-risk; FQ if carbapenem-allergic
Imipenem-cilastatin500 mg IV q6hRenal-dose; higher seizure riskCarbapenem alternative to meropenemMeropenem preferred if seizure risk
Levofloxacin750 mg IV q24hRenal-dose; QT/tendon cautionAntipseudomonal FQ; good lung penetration; non-β-lactam backbone optionUse as the β-lactam-free backbone in true penicillin allergy
Prior/home regimen or antibiogram unknown?Treat as MDR-risk: go straight to dual antipseudomonal coverage + empiric MRSA coverage, then de-escalate at 48–72 h on cultures. The guideline explicitly says use two agents when the local antibiogram is unavailable.
2
Add MRSA coverage
Prior IV abx <90 d, unit MRSA >10–20%/unknown, or high mortality risk.
▾
DrugStartTarget / adjustWhy it worksIf allergic / alt
Vancomycin15 mg/kg IV q8–12h (actual body wt); load 25–30 mg/kg if severe/critically illTarget AUC₂₄/MIC 400–600 (or trough 15–20); renal-dose, monitor AKIGlycopeptide — binds D-Ala-D-Ala, blocks cell-wall cross-linking in MRSALinezolid (esp. if renal-fragile or vanc allergy)
Linezolid600 mg IV q12hNo renal adjustment; watch platelets, serotonin syndromeOxazolidinone — 50S ribosome, stops MRSA protein synthesis; higher lung levelsVancomycin; ZEPHyR showed linezolid ≥ vanc for cure & less nephrotoxicity
Vancomycin and linezolid are co-equal first-line for MRSA nosocomial pneumonia. Prefer linezolid when the kidneys are fragile or vancomycin+pip-tazo would stack AKI risk; prefer vancomycin when serotonergic drug interactions or thrombocytopenia make linezolid awkward. A negative MRSA nares PCR lets you stop MRSA coverage early.
3
Dual antipseudomonal (different classes) + MRSA
MDR risk, structural lung disease, >10% unit GNR resistance, or antibiogram unknown.
▾

Keep the β-lactam backbone and add a second gram-negative agent from a different class (never two β-lactams). Goal: ≥1 active drug while susceptibilities return.

Second GNR agentStartAdjust / maxWhy it worksCaution
Ciprofloxacin400 mg IV q8hRenal-doseFQ — DNA gyrase; different class from β-lactamQT, tendinopathy, C. diff
Levofloxacin750 mg IV q24hRenal-doseFQ backbone alternativeQT, dysglycemia
Amikacin15–20 mg/kg IV q24hLevel-guided; short courseAminoglycoside — 30S ribosome; concentration-dependent GNR killNephro/ototoxic; never monotherapy (poor lung penetration)
Tobramycin / Gentamicin5–7 mg/kg IV q24hExtended-interval; level-guidedAminoglycoside second GNR agentSame toxicity caveats; reassess early
Aztreonam2 g IV q8hRenal-doseMonobactam — gram-negative only; safe in severe β-lactam allergyNo gram-positive/anaerobe cover; avoid pairing w/ ceftazidime (shared side chain)
For known/suspected MDR gram-negatives (CRE, MDR Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter): escalate with ID to ceftolozane-tazobactam 3 g q8h (ASPECT-NP), ceftazidime-avibactam 2.5 g q8h, meropenem-vaborbactam, imipenem-relebactam, cefiderocol, or colistin/polymyxin B salvage (± inhaled adjunct). These are ICU-level, antibiogram-driven choices.
Empiric HAP/VAP antibiotic decision tree — MRSA cover and single-vs-dual antipseudomonal coverage keyed to risk factors, then de-escalate. Source: IDSA/ATS 2016 (Kalil).
Duration & de-escalation7 days is the default for HAP and VAP regardless of organism (Kalil 2016; Chastre 2003) — extend only for slow clinical/radiologic/lab response or specific situations. De-escalate at 48–72 h to the narrowest agent the cultures allow, and use procalcitonin + clinical criteria to help stop. Source: IDSA/ATS 2016.

Interactions

Comorbidities & drugs to avoid

⚠️

How comorbidities change management

ComorbidityEffect on courseEffect on management
CKD / AKIReduced clearance → toxicity; cefepime encephalopathy riskRenal-dose vancomycin (level-guided), β-lactams, carbapenems, aztreonam; often avoid/extend aminoglycosides. Linezolid needs no renal adjustment — favor it.
Structural lung disease (bronchiectasis/CF)Chronic Pseudomonas colonization → higher MDR riskAssume Pseudomonas; use double antipseudomonal coverage.
ObesityAltered volume of distributionVancomycin on actual body weight (cap load ~3 g); aminoglycosides on adjusted body weight; favor extended/continuous β-lactam infusion for time>MIC.
ImmunosuppressionBroader differential, worse outcomesConsider fungal/viral/Pneumocystis/Nocardia; lower threshold for CT + invasive sampling.
On serotonergic drugs (SSRIs/SNRIs/tramadol)—Linezolid is a reversible MAOI → serotonin syndrome risk; prefer vancomycin or hold/space the serotonergic agent.
Cardiac / QT prolongation—Caution with fluoroquinolones (QT, arrhythmia); check the med list & electrolytes.
Drugs to avoid / use with caution: Vancomycin + piperacillin-tazobactam together — synergistic nephrotoxicity (↑AKI vs vanc alone or vanc+cefepime/meropenem); use vanc+cefepime/meropenem or switch to linezolid in fragile kidneys. Aminoglycoside monotherapy for pneumonia — poor lung penetration, never a sole agent. Linezolid + MAOIs/serotonergic agents — serotonin syndrome. Unadjusted cefepime in renal failure — neurotoxicity/nonconvulsive status. Two β-lactams as your “double coverage” — the second agent must be a different class.
Monitor

What to trend daily

📈

Daily reassessment

  • Oxygenation & work of breathing: SpO₂/FiO₂, respiratory rate — the earliest sign of failure or of response.
  • Temperature & WBC trend: expect improvement by 48–72 h.
  • Hemodynamics: MAP, lactate clearance, urine output, pressor need.
  • Cultures & susceptibilities: de-escalate the moment they allow; stop MRSA cover if nares PCR/cultures negative.
  • Renal function & drug levels: daily creatinine on vancomycin/aminoglycosides; AUC-guided vancomycin.
  • Procalcitonin trend: a falling PCT plus clinical improvement supports stopping.
Not improving by 72 h? Run the structured workup: wrong bug (resistant/atypical/fungal/viral), wrong drug (dose, penetration, source control), wrong diagnosis (PE, ARDS, atelectasis, aspiration pneumonitis, CHF), or a complication (empyema, abscess, extrapulmonary focus). Repeat imaging (CT), repeat cultures, involve ID. Do not reflexively broaden in the first 48–72 h if stable and cultures are pending.
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Floor → ICU triggers (numeric)

Transfer to ICU for any of: need for mechanical ventilation (or NIV failing) · PaO₂/FiO₂ <150 or refractory hypoxemia despite high-flow/NIV · septic shock — vasopressors to keep MAP ≥65 and lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluids · respiratory rate persistently ≥30 with rising work of breathing or hypercapnia · ≥3 minor severe-pneumonia criteria (RR ≥30, P:F ≤250, multilobar infiltrates, confusion, uremia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, hypothermia, hypotension needing aggressive fluids) · lactate rising despite resuscitation.

Thresholds: Surviving Sepsis 2021 (shock/MAP/lactate); ATS/IDSA 2019 CAP severe-pneumonia minor criteria (extrapolated for site-of-care); ARDS Berlin (P:F).

Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: afebrile trend, hemodynamically stable off pressors, adequate oxygenation on room air or stable home O₂, tolerating oral intake and an oral or completing IV regimen, improving WBC/infiltrate, and a clear plan to finish the 7-day course. Confirm de-escalation to the narrowest effective agent.

Home

Stable, self-caring, can complete oral antibiotics; reliable follow-up.

Home health

Home + skilled nursing/OPAT for IV completion, wound/line care.

SNF

Needs 24 h skilled nursing (IV abx, deconditioning), <3 h therapy/day.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Can tolerate ≥3 h therapy/day, ≥2 disciplines — post-critical-illness reconditioning.

LTAC

Prolonged complex care — ventilator weaning, long IV courses >25 days.

Hospice / palliative

Recurrent aspiration PNA in advanced illness — comfort-focused, goals of care.
🫀 ICU — ventilator-associated & severe hospital-acquired pneumonia
Admit

ICU triggers & VAP recognition

🚨

When it belongs in the unit

VAP = new pneumonia >48 h after intubation; suspect it when a ventilated patient develops a new infiltrate plus rising FiO₂/PEEP, purulent secretions, fever/leukocytosis. Severe HAP reaches the ICU for respiratory failure or shock.

ICU criteria: need for invasive ventilation, septic shock on vasopressors, PaO₂/FiO₂ <150/refractory hypoxemia, or ≥3 minor severe-pneumonia criteria. Both “need for ventilatory support due to the pneumonia” and “septic shock” also define high mortality risk, which mandates broad empiric coverage (MRSA + double antipseudomonal).
In septic shock or high-probability sepsis, give empiric antibiotics within 1 hour of recognition (Surviving Sepsis 2021) and draw cultures first only if it does not delay therapy.
Monitor

Monitoring, access & sampling

🩸

Lines, labs, and respiratory sampling

  • Access: central venous catheter for vasopressors/central labs; arterial line for continuous BP and frequent ABGs on the ventilated patient.
  • Trend: MAP (target ≥65), lactate clearance, urine output, ABG/P:F ratio, ventilator settings (FiO₂, PEEP, plateau), temperature/WBC, culture data, renal function & drug levels.
  • Respiratory sampling: the guideline prefers noninvasive endotracheal aspirate + semiquantitative culture over invasive BAL/PSB — it doesn’t change mortality or antibiotic days. If invasive is done: BAL ≥10⁴, PSB ≥10³, endotracheal aspirate ≥10⁵–10⁶ CFU/mL define a positive quantitative culture.
Bronchoscopic BAL. Invasive quantitative sampling is an option but not preferred — it doesn’t improve outcomes over endotracheal aspirate (Canadian CCTG, NEJM 2006).

Score

Sepsis screen — qSOFA

🧮

qSOFA (interactive)

Rapid bedside screen for poor outcome in suspected infection (Sepsis-3, Singer JAMA 2016). 1 point each; ≥2 flags high risk and should prompt escalation and a full SOFA assessment. Not a rule-out.

Respiratory rate ≥22/min
Altered mentation (GCS <15)
Systolic BP ≤100 mmHg
0
Select the criteria that apply.

Septic shock (Sepsis-3) = vasopressors needed for MAP ≥65 and lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluids. The full SOFA score is a continuous multi-organ nomogram — compute SOFA on MDCalc →.

Support

Pressors & sepsis bundle

💉

Which drip, why, and the dose

Septic shock from HAP/VAP follows Surviving Sepsis 2021: antibiotics within 1 h, ≥30 mL/kg crystalloid within 3 h for hypoperfusion, target MAP ≥65.

AgentReceptors / mechanismDose rangeHemodynamic effectWhen to pick
Norepinephrineα1 > β10.05–3 mcg/kg/min (titrate)↑SVR, mild ↑COFirst-line vasopressor in septic shock
VasopressinV1 receptor (non-catecholamine)Fixed 0.03 units/min↑SVR, catecholamine-sparingAdd when norepi rising (~0.25–0.5 mcg/kg/min)
Epinephrineβ1 = α1 (β2)0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑CO, ↑SVR, ↑HRAdd if MAP still inadequate on norepi+vaso
HydrocortisoneGlucocorticoid (vascular tone)200 mg/day (50 mg IV q6h or infusion)Restores vasopressor responsivenessRefractory shock on ongoing vasopressors
norepinephrine’s α1 effect restores the systemic vascular resistance that cytokine-driven vasodilation destroyed, while its mild β1 support maintains cardiac output — the exact hemodynamic lesion of distributive septic shock. Vasopressin adds non-catecholamine tone to spare escalating catecholamine dose.
Airway

Ventilation & lung protection

🌬️

NIV vs intubate; ARDSNet settings

A trial of NIV/high-flow can work for milder hypoxemic HAP, but intubate for refractory hypoxemia (P:F falling <150), rising work of breathing, hypercapnic failure, shock, or inability to protect the airway — don’t let a failing NIV trial delay it. Once VAP/ARDS supervenes, ventilate lung-protectively (ARDSNet).

Mechanically ventilated ICU patients. Endotracheal intubation and prolonged ventilation are the dominant VAP risk factors — every ventilated day adds risk.
Gustavo Basso · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons
VAP prevention bundleHOB 30–45° (semi-recumbent) · daily sedation interruption + spontaneous breathing trials to cut ventilator days · subglottic-secretion-drainage ET tubes · cuff pressure 20–30 cmH₂O · DVT and stress-ulcer prophylaxis · hand hygiene · avoid unnecessary reintubation. Chlorhexidine oral care is now controversial (a possible mortality signal in meta-analyses) — follow current local policy.
Rescue

Advanced / MDR & refractory options

⚙️

Resistant organisms & refractory hypoxemia

AgentDoseTargetWhy it worksNote
Ceftolozane-tazobactam3 g IV q8h (HAP/VAP dose)MDR PseudomonasAntipseudomonal cephalosporin + BLINon-inferior to meropenem in ASPECT-NP

Cefiderocol2 g IV q8hCarbapenem-resistant GNR, Acinetobacter, StenotrophomonasSiderophore cephalosporin — “Trojan-horse” iron uptakeReserve; ID-directed
Colistin / Polymyxin BColistin: load 5 mg/kg CBA, then ~5 mg/kg/day ÷ q12h · Polymyxin B: load 2–2.5 mg/kg, then 1.25–1.5 mg/kg q12hMDR gram-neg salvageDisrupt LPS outer membraneNephrotoxic; ± inhaled adjunct

Refractory hypoxemia (ARDS from VAP): optimize PEEP, deep sedation ± neuromuscular blockade for severe ARDS, prone positioning for P:F <150, and VV-ECMO referral for refractory cases at an ECMO center. Source control matters — drain empyema, treat abscess.

Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Step down when: off vasopressors ≥24 h with MAP ≥65 and cleared lactate · extubated or stable on minimal support (FiO₂ ≤0.4, PEEP ≤5–8) with adequate P:F · improving oxygenation, WBC and infiltrate · antibiotics de-escalated to a culture-directed narrow regimen with a defined stop date. Not yet if the patient still needs escalating pressors, has an unresolved source (undrained empyema), a rising oxygen requirement, or persistent hemodynamic lability.

Floor / step-down

Stable off pressors, secure airway, completing therapy.

LTAC

Prolonged ventilator weaning or long IV MDR course.

Palliative / hospice

Recurrent VAP in advanced illness — reframe goals of care.
